transcript.text: Hi, my Hotpoint Aquarius dryer is taking forever to dry and the top gets really hot. Model is TCM580GUK if that helps

A Hotpoint Aquarius TCM580GUK is a condenser dryer. When it takes ages to dry but gets very hot on top, the most common cause is restricted airflow. If air can't flow freely through the lint filter and condenser, the heat builds up inside (making the casing hot) and the drying becomes inefficient. Please do these two checks first:
1. Clean the fluff filter in the door opening.
2. Open the small flap at the bottom front to access the condenser unit, take it out, and rinse off any grey sludge or fluff under a tap. Let it drip dry before putting it back. Did you find either of these clogged with fluff?

Yes, both were clogged. The door filter had a thick layer of fluff on it (I'll admit I sometimes forget to clean it), and the condenser at the bottom had lint packed on the fins. I rinsed the condenser and it looks much cleaner now. Also, the top of the dryer gets very hot to the touch, and I often run it while I'm out at work.

It’s very common for a clogged filter and condenser to cause exactly this: the dryer overheats because air can’t escape, which makes the casing hot but stops the clothes from drying. Since you’ve cleaned both, that restriction is likely gone. However, running it unattended while you’re at work means it may have tripped its internal safety cut-out (thermal fuse) due to the earlier blockage, or the heater element itself could have failed. To tell which, please run a normal heat programme for about 10–15 minutes and carefully check if the air coming out of the rear vent is warm or hot. If it’s still cool after that time, the dryer isn’t heating at all, and we’ll need to look at the heater element or thermal cut-out. If it is hot but clothes are still damp, we should check the exhaust hose for a blockage.

I'm not sure how to check that, as I don't think my dryer has a vent or hose at the back (it's a condenser model). What I can say is that the drum turns and it does heat up, and the top panel gets very hot. The water container also collects water as normal. Does that help narrow it down?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. You're right that condenser dryers don't have an external vent hose – they recirculate air internally and pump the condensed water into your container. Since it is heating up and collecting water properly, the main issue is likely either residual airflow restriction or dirty moisture sensors. Even after rinsing, if the condenser fins are slightly bent or not perfectly dry when refitted, airflow can still be restricted. More commonly though, fabric conditioner builds up on the two metal sensor strips inside the drum (usually near where the filter sits), causing the dryer to think clothes are damp even when they aren't. Please wipe those sensor strips with a damp cloth and a little white vinegar to remove any coating. Also, check that you're not overloading the machine – it should only be about two-thirds full. Run another cycle after doing this.

Thanks, I'll wipe the sensor strips. The load is a normal size from a 1400 spin washer, so I don't think it's overloaded. It's also in a small utility room where the door is usually shut, if that matters. Is the very hot top panel something I should be worried about?

To answer your question: yes, the top getting very hot is a sign of restricted airflow. It’s not usually dangerous if the safety cut-outs work, but it means the dryer isn’t running efficiently. Then run one full cycle with the door open and see if the clothes come out dry in a normal time.

Thank you. I'll try that. The dryer is about 12 to 14 years old and came with the house, and there's a faint warm, dusty smell in the room when it runs. Should I keep running it while I'm out at work, or is there anything else I should check about its safety?

Given its age, I would strongly advise against leaving it running unattended while you are at work. The 'dusty smell' combined with the extreme heat suggests that dust has built up inside the casing or on the heating element itself, which is a fire risk as well as an efficiency killer. At this stage, it is safest to have an engineer inspect it; they can safely dismantle the casing to clean out that internal dust and check if the thermal cut-out (the safety device) has degraded.

candidates: Blocked airflow (lint filter or condenser) causing overheating and poor drying (high)
Faulty heater element or thermal cut-out (low)
